question_patterns_used.name: Physical-quantity estimation
question_patterns_used.lesson_response: Teaches benchmark choice, scale comparison, bracketing, unit retention, and a real-world plausibility check before a simple approximate record.

questions_visited.why_selected: Tests a familiar mass over five orders of magnitude.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Choose a plausible mass and reject implausible scales.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Compare a loaded bag with familiar loads, then eliminate gram-scale and person-scale values.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Treating any numerical value with kg as reasonable, especially 0.005 kg or 500 kg.

questions_visited.why_selected: Adds a time estimate so the lesson does not treat estimation as mass only.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Judge a sub-second event by lived experience.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Picture a blink and compare it with a noticeable second and a much longer wait.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Confusing a very brief but observable event with millisecond or tens-of-seconds scales.
lesson_sections_informed: Estimate a short time by comparing events
Worked example: time for ten taps

questions_visited.why_selected: Adds a three-dimensional comparison route with cubic units.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Use an imagined cube to identify a plausible object volume.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Find the rough box scale, then allow for the rounded object occupying less than the full box.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Choosing a volume that ignores the third dimension or is far too small or large.
lesson_sections_informed: A spatial estimate can use a simple shape
Worked example: volume of a melon

questions_visited.why_selected: Requires the reason behind an estimate, not only a final number.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Name a benchmark, compare it with a doorway, and justify a metre-scale estimate.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Bracket a door between ruler scale and building scale, then choose a human-height comparison.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Giving an unsupported remembered number with no physical comparison.
lesson_sections_informed: Bracket the scale before choosing a value

questions_visited.why_selected: Uses a repeated benchmark and requires a separate plausibility check.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Scale an estimated one-object mass to a group and explain why the result remains approximate.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Multiply a rough one-book mass by the number of books, retain kg, then compare with a liftable bundle.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Reporting an exact-looking product without acknowledging that the starting benchmark was estimated.

questions_visited.why_selected: Combines three approximate dimensions with the previous lesson's magnitude-and-unit record.
questions_visited.assessed_demand: Estimate a volume, identify its numerical magnitude and unit, and use a cube as a scale check.
questions_visited.reasoning_route: Multiply the three approximate dimensions, keep cubic centimetres, then compare the result with a reference cube.
questions_visited.misconception_or_distractor: Giving a bare number, losing a dimension, or accepting an untested volume scale.
lesson_sections_informed: A spatial estimate can use a simple shape
When an estimate is not a guess
